food.text: Between 450 BCE and 950 CE, pre-Columbian farming communities in the Amazon Basin created terra preta, a very dark, fertile soil. They made it by adding charcoal, bones, broken pottery, compost and manure to the low fertility Amazonian soil.

The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajó island at the mouth of the Amazon River, apparently between 800 AD and 1400 AD. It may have supported a population as large as 100,000, possibly using terra preta to make land suitable for large-scale agriculture.

In Brazil, shell middens known as sambaquis were created over a long period, from the 6th millennium BCE to the beginning of European colonisation. Because they hold a detailed record of what food was eaten or processed, they are invaluable to archaeologists.

Many terra preta soils are now thought to have formed under kitchen middens. Residues from food preparation, cooking fires, animal and fish bones and broken pottery piled up near living quarters. Other terra preta was made intentionally on larger scales.

Plant remains on Marajó show a diet built on small seed crops and small fish, which were either cultivated or protected by the people. Açai and tucuma palms added important supplements and also supplied material for baskets and canoes.

The charcoal in terra preta is stable and can remain in the soil for thousands of years, binding and retaining minerals and nutrients. Soil depths can reach 2 meters, and the soil is reported to regenerate itself at 1 centimeter per year.

Human remains show that the people of Marajó limited their consumption of starchy root crops like manioc. The heavy wear on their teeth suggests a diet based mainly on seed crops, tree fruits and fish.

Marajoara mounds held malocas, multi-family longhouses with several hearths lined up along the center, each likely serving one family. They had permanent cooking facilities of baked clay, and at Os Camutins up to 20 structures were built atop one another.

Stone griddles, which would suggest root crop processing, are very rare at Teso Dos Bichos, where Anna Roosevelt excavated. Their rarity is another sign that root crops were largely absent from the diet on Marajó.

art.text: On Marajó island, at the mouth of the Amazon River, the Marajoara culture made large pottery that was elaborately painted and incised with representations of plants and animals. Charles C. Mann suggests the culture flourished between 800 AD and 1400 AD, based on archeological studies.

Marajoara pottery gave archaeologists the first evidence that a complex society had existed on Marajó. Mound building points the same way, since only well-populated, sophisticated settlements were believed capable of such major earthworks.

Marajoara artisans made far more than vessels. Their output included figurines, large statues, pubic covers, pendants, ear and lip jewelry, whistles and spindle whorls. They also made ceramic miniatures of axes, mashers and hammers.

One of the best-known Marajoara forms is the globular urn, painted and modeled with anthropomorphic figures that represent primates. Other urns combine painting, incisions, excisions and modeling to show both human-like and animal figures.

Stone tools were very rare on Marajó island because it has no source of suitable stone. The few lithics that have been found suggest they were used as high-status items and gifts, or in craft production. Elaborate pottery vessels were found in garbage fills between houses and in graves, but not around hearths, which held only plain domestic wares.

Some Marajoara vases were decorated with painted geometric patterns. Simpler forms include bowls, while more complex ones include double-base vases, small statues, plates and bowls on pedestals. The funerary urns held the dead: when a significant person died, the flesh was cleared from their bones and the remains were placed in an urn, which was then topped with a bowl or platter.

science.text: Long before European contact, Amazonian farming communities turned poor forest soil into fertile black earth called terra preta. They mixed charcoal, bones, broken pottery, compost and manure into it. These soils were created between 450 BCE and 950 CE.

The Casarabe culture (c. 500–1400 AD) built stepped platforms, rectangular platform mounds and conical pyramids out of rammed earth, some as tall as 22 metres. It developed in parallel with the Tiwanaku state, in the Amazon lowlands of Bolivia.

The charcoal in terra preta is stable and stays in the soil for thousands of years. It binds and retains minerals and nutrients. This was a product of indigenous Amazonian soil management and slash-and-char agriculture.

Amazon rainforest peoples may have used their method of developing and working in terra preta to make the land suitable for large-scale agriculture. Such farming was needed to support large populations and complex social formations such as chiefdoms.

A research team led by Heiko Prümers used lidar technology to survey 67 Casarabe settlements in the Bolivian Amazon lowlands. The study presented in 2022 revealed two large sites covering 147 and 315 hectares, showing an advanced agrarian society.

Lidar mapping of the Casarabe culture found 92 sites, 61 of which had defensive structures. It also recorded terraces, straight causeways, water reservoirs and around 1,000 kilometres of canals and raised causeways that connected the sites.

Sombroek and colleagues estimate that terra preta covers at least 0.1–0.3% of low forested Amazonia, or 6,300 to 18,900 square kilometres. Others put the figure at 10.0% or more, which would be twice the area of Great Britain.

Recent research suggests terra preta may have a natural origin. Pre-Columbian people may have intentionally used and improved patches of existing soil fertility scattered among areas of lower fertility.

Farming technology at Marajó was limited mainly to stone axes, introduced in the Marajoara Phase. Stone griddles found at Teso Dos Bichos during Roosevelt's excavations are very rare, which is another marker of the absence of root crops from the diet. Teeth from human remains show heavy wear, suggesting people lived mainly on seed crops, tree fruits and fish.

politics.text: The Llanos de Moxos in Bolivia are covered with earthworks, yet so far there is no evidence that their inhabitants were politically united in pre-Columbian times. Instead they seem to have been organized into a large number of small, independent polities.

The Marajoara culture of Marajó island, at the mouth of the Amazon River, may have developed social stratification and supported a population as large as 100,000 people. Charles C. Mann suggests it flourished between 800 AD and 1400 AD. Skeletons point to a divide between elites and commoners: some individuals were well-nourished and tall, while others were significantly shorter and ate poorer diets, and some of the well-nourished had deformed skulls. Only a few individuals have been examined, though.

The Casarabe culture (c. 500-1400 AD) built a dense settlement network in the Llanos de Moxos. Remote sensing revealed over 189 earthen settlement mounds joined by causeways and canals across at least 4,500 km2. Recent research suggests a society of at least 10,000 people.

A research team led by Heiko Prümers used lidar to survey Casarabe sites in the Bolivian Amazon lowlands. Of 92 sites located, 61 had defensive structures. Enclosures with checkpoints were also recorded, hinting at organized control of movement and defense.

Around 1,000 kilometres of canals and raised causeways documented so far connected the Casarabe sites with one another. The sites of Cotoca and Landívar were primary centres in the settlement network.

Some scholars believe the Casarabe culture practiced a form of agrarian urbanism, based on the complexity of its earthworks. Others have postulated that a small population could have built these earthworks slowly over a long period of time.

Archaeologist Betty Meggers asserted that the Amazon Basin could not sustain a large population and that its inhabitants were hunter-gatherer bands or slash-and-burn farmers. The remains in the Llanos de Moxos testify to a well-organized and numerous indigenous people, contradicting her view.

philosophy.text: The belief system of the Marajo people, who lived on an island at the mouth of the Amazon, is not wholly understood. It almost certainly involved important female figures. Their iconography and art portray women with shamanistic powers and roles. It is possible that ancestor worship was very important, as the dead were placed in urns and buried in the mounds where the living also made their homes.

Marajoara settlements were aligned east to west, which fits an Amazonian cosmology that sees the universe as divided by gender. In that view, men are related to the sun and women to the moon. The layout of their villages may have echoed how they understood the cosmos.

Ancestor worship may have been very important to the Marajoarans. When a person of significance died, the flesh was cleared from their bones and the remains were placed in a large, elaborately decorated urn, topped with a bowl or platter. The urns were buried in the floors of houses built on the mounds, so the living and the dead shared the same ground.

Marajoara art may reflect a society that reckons descent through a mythical female ancestor. In Amazonian cosmology, ancestral females are regarded as creators, and Marajoaran iconography may represent them. This would tie the culture's images of women to its ideas about how the world began.

Among the Mapuche of south-central Chile and Argentina, the moon and the sun are spouses, as they are among Central Andean peoples. The Mapuche, Quechua and Aymara words for the sun and moon appear to be borrowed from Puquina. This suggests the shared cosmology may go back to the days of the Tiwanaku Empire.

culture.text: The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajó in the Amazon delta from AD 400 to 1400. It developed sophisticated pottery, social stratification, large populations and mound building. It also built complex social formations such as chiefdoms.

Amazonian farmers made a very dark, fertile soil called terra preta, meaning "black earth". They added charcoal, bones, broken pottery, compost and manure to the poor Amazonian soil. Communities created it between 450 BCE and 950 CE.

Among the Marajoara, the more elaborate artifacts were intended for funerary or ritual use, while everyday objects were decorated less elaborately. The largest and most beautiful pieces are funerary urns, buried in house floors on top of the mounds. When a significant individual died, the flesh was cleared from their bones and the remains were placed in the urn, which was topped with a bowl or platter.

Women appear prominently in Marajoara art, portrayed as creators and lineage heroes or founders. Households were matrilocal, and women were important in subsistence production. Evidence about their status is mixed, so interpretations of Marajoara society are difficult to define.

Terra preta's charcoal is stable and stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding and retaining nutrients. Ordinary cleared Amazon soils are productive only briefly before rain or flooding leach the nutrients away. Farmers must then clear a new area, but terra preta resists this leaching.
Terra preta soils can reach depths of 2 meters. The soil is reported to regenerate itself at a rate of 1 centimeter per year. This is unusual, since most cleared Amazon soils are quickly exhausted.

Marajoara mounds held malocas, Amazonian longhouses built of earth, wooden poles and thatch. They were occupied continually, with up to 20 structures built atop one another at places such as Os Camutins. Cooking facilities were made of baked clay, and plastered floors were frequently repaired.

Recent research suggests terra preta may be of natural origin. If so, pre-Columbian people intentionally used and improved existing patches of soil fertility scattered among areas of lower fertility. This challenges the idea that all of it was made from scratch.
